For most of her junior career, Mira Okafor won points in spite of her serve [s:mag]. It was slow, it was predictable and opponents stepped in to attack it.

## Growing up in Leeds

She started at a public park court in Leeds where the nets sagged and the lines had faded to suggestions. Her mother, a nurse, booked the court on Saturday mornings because it was cheap. A county coach spotted her at a summer camp when she was nine [s:tour]. She was quick, she hated losing and she talked to herself between points. All three habits stayed.

## Junior years

As a junior she reached a top-twenty ranking and a Grand Slam junior quarter-final [s:tour]. Good, not exceptional. Several coaches suggested she lacked a weapon. She agreed, privately, and spent a year she describes as boring and necessary changing her service motion from the ground up [s:mag].

## The new serve

The fix was mostly in the legs. She had been arming the ball. A coach in Spain had her serve hundreds of balls from her knees to feel the shoulder turn, then added the leg drive back in. Her first-serve speed rose by about 15 km/h within a season and her double faults fell [s:mag]. Her return game had always been strong. Now she could hold serve.

## Breakthrough

In 2025 she won her first tour title on grass, beating two seeded players on the way, and climbed into the top fifty [s:tour]. Grass suits her. The low bounce rewards her flat backhand, and the short points hide what is still an average second serve.

She is honest about that. "It's better," she told an interviewer. "It isn't good yet." [s:mag]

## Playing style

Okafor plays close to the baseline and takes the ball early. Her forehand is heavy rather than fast; her backhand is the shot opponents fear, struck flat and often down the line [s:tour]. On clay she has struggled to finish points, and her record on the surface is still below fifty per cent. Coaches who have worked with her describe a player who studies opponents closely and changes tactics mid-match, sometimes too often.
